item.title: When the Places That Heal Us Are Burning
item.description:
Grief

When the Places That Heal Us Are Burning

Climate grief may be the cost of deeply loving the places that help us heal.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Natural landscapes help humans heal
  • Place attachment describes the emotional bonds that humans develop with particular environments.
  • Climate change introduces anticipatory grief into our love of wild places in nature.
  • The outdoors is where many of us go when life becomes too much. But this may expose us to climate anxiety.
Source: Enea Rezhda via Unsplash

When I learned that a wildfire was moving toward the treehouse that my sister and I had built together as children, I felt a pit in my stomach. My sister died unexpectedly not long after we built it, and over the years, the treehouse became one of the few tangible pieces of our childhood together that remained. We had nailed wooden ladder rungs up the trunk. The snack shelves we built while arguing about which snacks to buy at the market. And we added a mailbox where we left each other letters, excitedly raising the little red flag to alert the other of what was waiting inside.

And then, many years later, a wildfire was moving toward it. I imagined the treehouse engulfed in flames and felt sick, like the wind had been knocked out of me. It was only later that I found language for what I was experiencing: I was grieving a place.

When a Landscape Becomes Part of You

Psychology has a language for why the potential loss of a treehouse—or a forest, mountain, or trail—can affect us so deeply. Place attachment describes the emotional bonds that humans develop with particular environments. Places accumulate memories: The trail you returned to when your life was falling apart. The mountain climb that showed you what your body could do. The lake that you and your children return to every summer. These places are not just interchangeable scenery; they become part of the stories of our lives. And seeing them threatened, or dramatically damaged, can bring about strong grief. Ecopsychologist Theodore Roszak argued for a psychology spacious enough to recognize our relationship with the Earth—a psyche, in essence, as big as the planet. If the landscapes we love become part of our psychological lives, perhaps it isn't surprising to grieve when they burn. The wound isn't entirely outside of us.

There Is a Name for Grieving a Place

The feeling that I experienced as that wildfire moved toward the treehouse can be understood as ecological grief. Researchers use the term to describe grief associated with the loss or anticipated loss of ecosystems, species, landscapes, and ways of life due to environmental change. Sometimes ecological grief arrives after a place is gone. Sometimes it arrives while we are terrified of losing it. Here in Oregon, this feeling is becoming too familiar. I find myself refreshing wildfire maps and seeing the places I love within red evacuation zones. Smoke filters the sun into an apocalyptic orange glow. I recognize the names of forests, mountains, rivers, and wilderness areas threatened by wildfires. These aren't simply places on a map to me. I have walked through them. They have witnessed my grief, moved me with their beauty, and challenged me as a hiker and climber.

article continues after advertisement

As an ecotherapist and former outdoor guide, I have spent years thinking about how landscapes help humans heal. When we are outside, our attention shifts. Anxious thought spirals can quiet. Awe draws us beyond ourselves. Our relationships to our bodies change. We connect with other people and with something larger than ourselves. But climate change has made me think more about the other side of that relationship: What happens when the place you go to heal becomes something you have to grieve?

Missing a Place While You're Still There

Environmental philosopher Glenn Albrecht coined the term solastalgia, to describe the distress people experience when a familiar environment changes around them and no longer feels the same. Many people around the world are experiencing this now. Increasingly, summers in the West carry this feeling. For many, summers involved trips to the river, camping, stargazing, walking outside, and picnics. Now summers are marked by smoke forecasts, extreme heat, closures, and air quality alerts. Before heading out on a climb, I find myself checking not only the weather, but also fire maps and the AQI.

And the changes are visible to those who pay close attention. We notice when snow disappears earlier in the season. We witness glaciers grow thinner each year. We remember what a forest looked like before it became a burn zone. Those of us who enjoy time in nature become firsthand witnesses to climate change. And now we wonder whether the landscapes we have enjoyed will still be around for our children.

Climate change introduces a strange anticipatory grief into our love of wild places in nature. We can anticipate that these places could be lost. Environments that once felt permanent suddenly face the vulnerability of destruction. To love a place is not without risk.

When Your Refuge Becomes Anxiety-Provoking

There is a painful paradox for those of us who rely on nature for our mental health. The outdoors is where many of us go when life becomes too much. But we can no longer enter those places without encountering evidence of the damage that climate change is causing. The place that calms my anxiety can now provoke another kind of anxiety.

article continues after advertisement

Eco-anxiety describes the stress related to climate change and environmental degradation. It includes feelings of fear, helplessness, anger, sadness, and worry about the future. These are valid, important feelings about a serious concern. Eco-anxiety is not a psychological problem that needs to be solved, but it does shine light on the evidence of our innate, intimate connection to nature.

The Cost of Loving a Place

I don’t think that the answer to climate grief is to pull away from nature as a means of emotional self-preservation. Or to try to care less. For me, the grief serves as a reminder to pay close attention and to savor the moments that I have. I notice as much as I can: The smell of the earth when it rains. The intricacies of wildflowers that grow alongside the trail. The frogs croaking in the meadow. The sense of wonder I feel when I see Mount Hood, the 500,000-year-old volcano in my backyard, knowing that it has witnessed a span of history that my mind can barely comprehend.

There is more tenderness in my relationship with nature now. And perhaps more urgency—to protect habitats, participate in climate solutions, and advocate for the preservation of public lands and places. I wish I could return to hiking without needing to reference wildfire maps. And I wish I could know that the landscapes that I love will look the same when my children are grown. But I cannot.

Perhaps loving nature simply requires that we pay attention and protect it. And when the places that have held our grief begin to disappear, to allow ourselves to grieve them, too.

item.title: The Mountain Never Told Me I Was Too Old
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

The Mountain Never Told Me I Was Too Old

Personal Perspective: A lesson in resilience from the world’s highest volcanoes.

Posted August 5, 2026

The biggest lie you'll ever believe is the story you tell yourself about what you're no longer capable of doing. Maybe you've heard it.

“You're too old.”

“It's too late.”

“You missed your chance.”

On an expedition in Argentina, I found myself listening to that voice.

In my 50s, I was preparing for an expedition to climb the highest volcanoes in the world in world-record time, repeatedly pushing above 22,000 feet into an environment where oxygen is scarce, and mistakes are amplified. I’ve spent decades climbing mountains, setting world records, and operating in extreme environments. On paper, I had every reason to feel confident.

Yet doubt showed up anyway. I had experience, but I was no longer 35.

As I studied weather patterns and planned routes, new questions crept in that would have seemed foreign years earlier. Would my body still adapt? Would I recover fast enough? Was I trying to hold on to a younger version of myself?

What struck me was how easily I was accepting the doubt as truth. This may well be a self-limiting belief or a self-fulfilling prophecy: a perception that constricts a person’s behavior before reality ever has a chance to weigh in. Many of the limits that shape our lives aren't physical; they're assumptions disguised as certainties.

The volcanoes exposed that truth quickly. The air was thin and brutally cold. The winds were intense. The terrain was rocky, snowy, and relentless. Every step demanded my focus. There was no room for distraction, excuses, or self-pity. And eventually, like in every meaningful challenge, I hit the moment:

“What the hell did I get myself into?”

It was not a cinematic, life-or-death moment. It’s just that my legs felt heavy. Fatigue began negotiating for my attention. Quitting started to sound reasonable. But that’s where resilience is built. We often think resilience is something you have or don't have. But resilience is a process, not so much a personality trait. It's choosing your next step instead of surrendering to discomfort.

When I stopped wishing conditions were easier and embraced the discomfort, I could focus on what needed to happen next.

Manage my energy. Stay present.

The mountain didn't care about my age. It didn't care about my accomplishments. It didn't care about my doubts. It simply demanded a response to the conditions before me. That’s when it stopped feeling like a battle against the mountain and started feeling like a conversation with myself.

This may well be adaptive resilience. This is the ability to respond effectively to changing demands rather than resisting them. The people who thrive later in life aren't necessarily the strongest, fastest, or most gifted. They're the most adaptable.

Success on the volcanoes didn't come from attacking the mountain harder. It came from listening, adjusting, and making good decisions repeatedly. In many ways, the same skills that help us navigate relationships, careers, wellness challenges, and life's fears.

article continues after advertisement

Yes, age mattered. But so did experience. Discipline. Perseverance. The qualities I’d been testing and worried about had evolved into strengths. And that's a lesson far bigger than mountaineering. You don't have to climb a volcano to find your edge. You may find it in a career transition, a health challenge, a relationship, or a long-delayed goal.

In those moments, it can feel like life is asking how much you can endure. But the better question is: Who are you becoming under pressure? Hardship doesn't just test you; it reveals you. It exposes the beliefs and truths you've been carrying. It shows you which beliefs are working and which are holding you back.

Standing on the highest volcano summits in the world, I didn’t celebrate the achievements. I realized the real obstacle had never been the mountain. It was the story I’d been telling myself. The mountains never told me I was too old. They never placed doubts within me to see if I still "had what it takes." I did.

We all have limits. But before we accept them, we can make sure they're real. Because sometimes the barrier standing between us and the next summit isn't age, condition, or ability. It's a story we've stopped questioning.

item.title: Rage Bait: An Angering, Yet Original Engagement Hack
item.description:
Creativity

Rage Bait: An Angering, Yet Original Engagement Hack

Posting enraging content fuels engagement through dark creativity.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Rage baiting is deliberately posting provocative content to infuriate users.
  • Rage bait posts combine originality with the goal to harm others by inducing anger.
  • Emotion-driven content hijacks the thinking brain and elicits a reaction through engagement.

I was re-watching The Office, like I usually do when higher-order cognition is elusive, and S05E03 (Business Ethics) had a classic Jim (portrayed by John Krasinski) prank on Dwight (Rainn Wilson). After Dwight claimed to have never stolen time from the company by attending to personal matters at work, Jim went to deliberately trigger Dwight into a non-work conversation:

Jim: By any chance, did you see Battlestar Galactica last night?

Andy (played by Ed Helms): No, I did not. Was that any good?

Jim: Actually, no. It was really so-so.

Dwight: Ok. [Dwight turns around, but Jim holds up the stopwatch, threatening to start it]

Jim: I mean, I like all the crazy monsters and stuff. You know, like Klingons and Wookies and all that, but... [Dwight begins to turn around again, Jim holds up the watch] Sorry, was there something you wanted to add, Dwight?

Andy: Is that anything like the original Battlestar Galactica?

Jim: You know, it's weird. It's practically a shot-for-shot remake.

Andy: Really? [Dwight closes his eyes, clutches the paper in his hands] Huh, that's cool.

Jim: Story's kinda bland. It's about this guy named Dumbledore Calrissian who needs to return the ring back to Mordor.

Even before rage-baiting was a term, Jim was needling Dwight to elicit a reaction, because angry people engage more with content that upsets them. Today, deliberate provocation online fuels engagement metrics, and these numbers transform into revenue from social media platforms. It’s an oddly beneficial tactic used by content creators. This post is less about how rage baiting works, and more about how darkly creative some of the rage bait content is.

Source: Manfred antranias Zimmer / Pixabay.

In the world of artificial intelligence (AI), the originality of rage bait (and other kinds of) posts is unlimited. I recently became a mom, again, and came across an outrageous post advertising Lull, which is an “autonomous infant mobility platform.” Obviously AI-generated, it was accompanied by a video of a mother placing her baby in a driverless vehicle and programming it to go to “dad’s house.” Touted as a failsafe solution for baby-transport because “babies sleep when the car moves,” it was an absurd idea that had one purpose: to invoke a reaction from sleep-deprived parents. There was another post about a Robopod “launched” by Tesla, which was an autonomous stroller, with an AI-generated mother awkwardly walking beside it. For me, the most infuriating part was the suggestion that the infants were happy to have no contact with their caregiver. I know it was fake and it was a rage bait post, but I felt irritated (and amused) nonetheless.

article continues after advertisement

Rage bait posts can be darkly creative, as their goal is to provoke and supersede our thinking brain into giving a visceral reaction. They are often rather original, even though they harm by way of inducing negative emotions.

Source: Omar Nasif / Pixabay

The content is often intentionally framed as novel, unique, or priceless, offering the bait to scrollers. Recommending strange food pairings as being the best in the world or making contentious claims about health trends can infuriate some users, who engage with these posts to express their counterpoints. Usually, no one gets brownie points for being correct on the Internet, but motivated users still try. Rage bait capitalises on this tendency and serves up creative and at times ridiculous posts that aim to instigate.

Emotion-driven content is highly clickable because it triggers users into having, if not sharing, an opinion about the post. It is also ingeniously creative because the more original the content, the more likely it is to enrage different users in different ways. Consider a post that not only discusses the merits of pineapple on pizza but also claims that garlic bread with pineapple puree makes for a great appetizer. Pizza purists will disagree wholeheartedly, and such a post would rake in the views and comments, all converting into big bucks for the poster. I would argue that the more absurd, weird, surprising, and enraging the post, the greater the engagement, making this a fertile ground for dark creativity. Given how online content is mushrooming, analysing rage bait content would be a great way to test this hypothesis.

item.title: When Levity Heals Rather Than Hurts
item.description:
Humor

When Levity Heals Rather Than Hurts

How lightheartedness can soften shame, ease tension, and deepen connection.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Healthy humor can soften shame and help us hold our imperfections with greater kindness.
  • Humor can deepen connection when it creates ease rather than distance or defensiveness.
  • Sarcasm often wounds, while playful humor can foster trust, repair, and connection.
  • Learning to smile at our humanity can reduce self-criticism and increase resilience.
Source: Pexels image by Thurman

Growing up in New York, I understand how humor can be hurtful. Sarcastic barbs that diminish a person are not humorous at all. Yet, held lightly, humor can soften painful edges, ease defensiveness, and bring a welcome spaciousness around life’s challenges.

The humor I’m referencing isn't about telling jokes in defensiveness—a strategy to deflect others’ displeasure with us. And it’s certainly not about disparaging anyone. It’s about bringing lightness into situations so we can hold them a little more gently. Well-placed humor can soften shame, reduce defensiveness, and help us stay connected to ourselves and others.

Healthy Humor Versus Defensive Humor

Sarcastic humor can wound. Our partner can’t find her keys, and we say: “You’d lose your head if it weren’t attached to your shoulders.” We’re late for a dinner date, and our partner is upset, and we respond: ‘It’s interesting how you don’t like it when I’m late, but you’re the one who’s slow getting out of the house when we want to go somewhere.” Such sarcasm can rupture trust and create distance.

Research by Rod Martin and colleagues found that affiliative and self-enhancing humor are associated with greater psychological well-being, while aggressive and self-defeating humor link to less healthy outcomes.

When you’re about to say something you think is humorous, pause for a moment and ask yourself:

  • Is my intention to be hurtful or to bring some lightheartedness to the situation?
  • If I'm being lighthearted, am I minimizing feelings, avoiding discomfort, or helping create ease and connection?
  • Am I feeling kind--or acting out my anger or displeasure indirectly?

Healthy Humor Toward Ourselves

Healthy humor has a way of disarming shame and softening our inner critic. It may take the form of self-amusement at our own foibles rather than harshly judging ourselves. Shopping at Costco one day, I felt annoyed when someone was blocking the aisle with his cart: “Doesn’t he realize people need to get through?” A few moments later, when I stopped my cart to peruse some items, a man turned to me and said good-naturedly, “May I get through?” Yikes! I was doing the very thing I was criticizing others for.

article continues after advertisement

As my self-image of being more thoughtful than others was rudely pierced, I experienced a moment of shame and self-criticism. What helped me recover my dignity was having a sense of amusement toward my foibles. I realized that I didn’t need to take my lapse of awareness of my surroundings so seriously or condemn myself. Although I intend to be mindful, like everyone, I’m quite capable of lapsing; I’m no better or worse than anyone else. A touch of humor with myself loosened my attachment to an idealized self-image and helped me find a greater measure of self-acceptance.

Once during a therapy session, I knocked over my glass of water, immediately followed by a profane utterance. Not only did I embarrass myself by spilling my water, but I dug myself into a deeper hole by my immediate reaction. Catching myself, I looked at my client with a wry smile: “Well, that wasn’t a very professional utterance!” Fortunately, my client smiled back at me in a spirit of acceptance. Humor can help defuse awkward situations and humanize us.

Humor can help us see things with more perspective. Being human, we’re all prone to making mistakes, being shortsighted, and sometimes acting in ways that spoil our self-image. When we can smile at our humanity rather than condemning ourselves, we can live with more ease and less self-seriousness.

Being Playful

Saying something playful at just the right moment can diffuse tensions and soften the interaction. It can help us release our rigid positions and offer a breath of fresh air, which can help with repair and maintain connection.

Bringing more playfulness into everyday life can make our relationships feel lighter, more enjoyable, and more connected.

Try this: if you eat meat or fish, next time you’re at the deli counter, ask for .61 or .97 lbs of whatever you order. The puzzled look—or smile—you receive from the unusual request may remind both of you that life doesn't always need to be so serious.

When someone you’re complimenting responds that you’re being too generous, you might respond: “Well, my motto is: let in a compliment whether we think we deserve it or not.”

You might experiment with other creative ways to bring a bit more playfulness and joy into your life and the lives of others.

Humor can be double-edged. Used carelessly, it can wound and create distance. Used wisely, it can soften shame, ease tension, and help us navigate life's challenges with greater perspective and grace. The humor that heals isn't about making people feel uncomfortable or minimizing painful situations. It's about sensing when the moment feels right to hold ourselves, our struggles, and one another with a little more lightness.

item.title: Nuances of Postpartum Psychosis — Physiology Over Psychology
item.description:
Psychosis

Nuances of Postpartum Psychosis — Physiology Over Psychology

The nuances of postpartum psychosis are keys to the resolution of the symptoms.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Postpartum psychosis reflects a whole-system physiologic event.
  • Prevention and treatment should include a whole-system approach.
  • The whole system extends beyond the body and mind to include the historical and present environment.
  • The current paradigm invoked to describe postpartum psychosis lacks nuance and is incomplete.

Postpartum psychosis can be understood as the most extreme expression of a nervous system that has become trapped in an unresolved, escalating threat state during one of the greatest physiological transitions of human life. A central premise in this perspective is that all psychology is physiology at its core. Emotions, behaviors, thoughts, perceptions, and beliefs are emergent properties of underlying mitochondrial, cellular, metabolic, endocrinologic, immunologic, and neurologic phenomena.

From this perspective, postpartum psychosis is not fundamentally a disease of thoughts. It is a disorder of whole-system physiology in which the brain begins constructing reality from a body that continues to signal danger after childbirth.

Pregnancy itself represents a progressively increasing physiological burden. As gestation advances, the growing fetus and placenta demand increasing metabolic resources, cardiovascular output, immune adaptation, endocrine regulation, and tissue remodeling. Near term, these demands, burden, and threats to the mother culminate in labor, an intentionally coordinated process characterized by a release of danger-associated peptides, cytokines, purines, prostaglandins, stress hormones, metabolic mobilization, and activation of innate immunity. The maternal organism temporarily shifts into a highly kinetic threat phenotype designed to accomplish delivery and protect both mother and infant.

Delivery removes the fetus and placenta, but it does not immediately remove the maternal threat state. Instead, the mother enters another demanding physiological phase characterized by tissue injury, uterine involution, wound repair, blood loss, pain, immune activation, metabolic depletion, hormonal withdrawal, lactation, and profound sleep disruption. Normally, these processes are followed by threat signaling resolution, a drop in inflammation, metabolic recovery, endocrine stabilization, healing, and return toward a safety phenotype.

The central question therefore becomes: Why do some mothers fail to resolve this acute threat response?

The nuance and the answer lie not solely within childbirth itself, but within the total cumulative threat load carried by the individual before, during, and after pregnancy.

Every individual develops within a dynamic lifelong environment composed of physical, emotional, mental, social, cultural, societal, financial, and spiritual influences. Chronic disease, pain, poverty, insecurity, conflict, abuse, discrimination, isolation, financial stress, and existential disconnection continually shape metabolic, endocrinologic, immunologic, neurologic, and psychologic regulation. Repeated exposure to threat conditions the entire system: It changes genetic expression, modifies stress regulation, alters immune responsiveness, modifies neurologic expression, sets psychologic status, and can produce enduring epigenetic and developmental changes that influence how future threats are perceived and resolved.

article continues after advertisement

The result is a biologic threat code—a physiological prediction about how dangerous the world is, how rapidly the organism should respond, how intensely it should defend itself, and how difficult it is to return to safety.

Pregnancy and childbirth occur within this physiological landscape.

For most women, the postpartum period provides sufficient signals of safety to terminate the inflammatory threat response. Oxytocin release, parasympathetic stimulation, social support, and mother-baby engagement are usually sufficient to turn the acute threat response off. Threat cytokines resolve. Tissue heals. Sleep returns. Hormones recalibrate. Metabolic reserves recover. The nervous system gradually transitions from survival toward connection and restoration.

For others, however, the embedded code and environment continue to communicate danger. Persistent pain, infection, blood loss, nutritional depletion, sleep deprivation, financial hardship, relationship conflict, social isolation, caregiving stress, uncertainty, and unresolved developmental or psychological threat continue to amplify the same biological pathways initiated during labor. Rather than receiving evidence that the emergency has ended, the maternal system continues to receive evidence that survival remains uncertain or that survival is even more precarious.

Inflammatory signaling persists. Purinergic and peptide danger signaling continues. Metabolic resources remain depleted. Endocrine shifts reduce stability. Circadian rhythms become fragmented. Brain functions change: Microglia-expressed threat bias, unstable monoamine regulation, enhanced glutamate signaling, impaired GABAergic balance, and disrupted cortical network integration may emerge as consequences of the continuing physiological threat state.

Within this framework, the brain is not malfunctioning randomly. It is adapting to the physiology it is receiving.

As cortical integration becomes increasingly impaired, evolutionarily newer networks responsible for executive function, flexible reasoning, self-reflection, and reality testing gradually lose regulatory control. Simultaneously, evolutionarily older systems involved in threat detection, autonomic regulation, emotional salience, survival behavior, thought bias, and defensive prediction assume increasing influence over perception and reaction.

article continues after advertisement

Reality itself becomes reorganized through a threat-biased physiological state.

Sleep deprivation further amplifies this process. Sleep is one of the primary biological mechanisms through which inflammation resolves, metabolism recovers, synaptic activity reorganizes, and cortical networks regain stability. When restorative sleep becomes impossible, inflammatory physiology persists, monoamine regulation becomes increasingly unstable, and the distinction between internally generated predictions and externally generated sensory information begins to deteriorate.

Psychotic symptoms emerge not because thoughts become diseased independently of the body, but because the physiological systems responsible for constructing a conscious cortical reality become progressively disorganized. Ordinary events acquire overwhelming significance. Neutral stimuli become interpreted as threats or messages. Fear becomes certainty. Internal thoughts become experienced as external voices. The brain attempts to construct coherent explanations for signals generated by a body that continues to communicate danger.

Importantly, the content of postpartum psychosis often reflects the individual's existing threat code. Delusions commonly involve persecution, contamination, religious themes, overwhelming responsibility, guilt, annihilation, and harm to the infant. These themes mirror the individual's deepest physiological predictions regarding survival, attachment, identity, and existence rather than appearing randomly.

The nuance outlined here proposes that postpartum psychosis is not simply an isolated psychiatric disorder. It represents the convergence of cumulative lifetime threat biology, acute reproductive threat physiology with inflammation, metabolic stress, endocrine transition, sleep disruption, and persistent environmental danger inputs into a self-amplifying whole-system threat phenotype.

The illness persists because the physiological system continues to receive evidence that threat remains unresolved. Recovery therefore requires restoring biological and experiential safety across multiple domains simultaneously. This results in resolving inflammation, reducing pain, restoring sleep, replenishing metabolic reserves, stabilizing endocrine function, sustaining interpersonal bonds, strengthening social connection, reducing environmental threat, rebuilding agency, and re-establishing a deep sense of security, attachment, and belonging.

Within this model, postpartum psychosis represents the extreme end of a continuum extending from adaptive acute threat physiology to persistent and chronic whole-system threat dysregulation. The organizing principle is simple: the brain can only generate cortical consciousness from the physiology it receives. When physiology remains organized around threat, cortical consciousness increasingly reflects threat. When physiology returns to safety, the brain regains the capacity for integration, connection, accurate perception, and healing.

article continues after advertisement

Postpartum psychosis is very much about a biologic and physiologic state more than a psychologic and characterologic state.
